data.conditions: non-pathogen-free, outdoor cages with running wheels, 29°C indoors

source.text: Both Acomys species (A. russatus and A. dimidiatus) originated from a colony at Tel Aviv University Zoological Research Garden... housed in large cages (70 cm by 50 cm by 65 cm) outdoors with running wheels and shelters, under non–pathogen-free conditions from 2018 to 2023.

Both Acomys species (A. russatus and A. dimidiatus) originated from a colony at Tel Aviv University Zoological Research Garden... housed in large cages (70 cm by 50 cm by 65 cm) outdoors with running wheels and shelters, under non–pathogen-free conditions from 2018 to 2023.

data.conditions: specific pathogen-free (SPF) at Yale School of Medicine

source.text: M. musculus (C57BL/6N) was supplied by the National Institute on Aging (NIA) and maintained under SPF conditions at Yale School of Medicine with ventilated cage racks.

data.conditions: 18-month-old male C57BL/6N, recombinant mouse clusterin 50 μg/kg daily for 2 weeks
18-month-old male C57BL/6N, saline daily for 2 weeks

data.hypothesis: A. russatus is protected from age-related functional decline
data.disproofExplanation: If A. russatus showed similar age-related decline as A. dimidiatus, hypothesis would be disproved.

data.hypothesis: Elevation of clusterin is an adaptive response that limits age-associated cellular or organismal damage
data.disproofExplanation: If clusterin elevation does not correlate with health span or if supplementation fails to improve health span, hypothesis would be weakened.

data.hypothesis: A. russatus might not develop a cellular senescence–like phenotype in the liver with aging
data.disproofExplanation: If aged A. russatus showed increased senescence markers, hypothesis would be disproved.

data.purpose: test effects of clusterin on health span in aged mice

source.text: Eighteen-month-old male C57BL/6N mice were intraperitoneally injected with vehicle (saline) or recombinant mouse clusterin (50 μg/kg) for 2 weeks
The cells were treated either with VEH (saline) or 5 μg/ml of ConA for 24 or 48 hours before analysis.

data.dosageRegimen: 1 hour pretreatment with clusterin, then LPS for 4 or 24 hours

source.text: Cells were stabilized at 37°C CO2 incubator and were pretreated with indicated doses of recombinant human clusterin (R&D Systems) for 1 hour. After that, LPS (1 μg/ml) was treated for 4 or 24 hours
A 4-mm ear punch was made using a caliper.

data.details: Open field, wire hanging, beam walking, novel object, T-maze tests performed on Acomys of varying ages

source.text: In 2022, Acomys of varying ages (0.5 to more than 3.5 years) underwent a series of behavioral tests.

data.details: 4-mm ear punch, area measured weekly for 5 weeks

source.text: Every 7 days, the ear punch area was measured under anesthesia, and the average area was calculated for each age and sex group.

data.details: H&E, Sirius Red, Sudan Black B staining of tissues

source.text: Sections were deparaffinized, washed, and stained for hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and Sirius Red staining.

data.details: Splenocytes treated with ConA, proliferation assessed by WST-8

source.text: Cell proliferation was assessed using the WST-8 cell proliferation assay kit (Abcam) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

data.details: Whole liver tissues collected, RNA isolated, sequenced on HiSeq 2500

source.text: Whole liver tissues were collected from three individual male M. musculus and A. russatus, aged either 0.5 or 2.5 years, and immediately snap frozen. Total RNA was isolated using QIAGEN RNeasy Mini kits and sequenced on a HiSeq 2500.

data.details: Epididymal white adipose tissues pooled, nuclei isolated, sequenced on HiSeq 3000

source.text: Snap-frozen epididymal white adipose tissues from 0.5- or 2.5-year-old M. musculus and 0.5- or 3.5-year-old A. russatus (n=3 per group) were pooled, and nuclei were isolated as previously described.

data.details: 18-month-old mice injected with clusterin or vehicle for 2 weeks, then health span and tissue analyses

source.text: For clusterin in vivo experiments, 18-month-old male mice were randomly assigned to treatment groups on the first day of the experiment.

data.details: BMDMs polarized to M1 or M2, then treated with clusterin

source.text: BMDMs were polarized into proinflammatory (M1) using recombinant mouse interferon-γ (20 ng/ml) and LPSs (1 μg/ml), or anti-inflammatory (M2) macrophages using recombinant mouse IL-4 (20 ng/ml), for 24 hours in RPMI 1640 medium without FBS.

data.details: CD14+CD16- monocytes isolated, pretreated with clusterin, then LPS

source.text: Frozen peripheral blood was thawed, and CD14+CD16− monocytes were isolated using the EasySep Human Monocyte Isolation Kit (StemCell Technologies), according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
Using this cohort, we explored age-related changes in various functional and behavioral outcomes.
To investigate this in our congeneric Acomys cohorts, we examined the age-related changes in regeneration capacity using a 4-mm ear punch assay.
We next investigated the spleens to understand the comparative immune aging of C57BL/6 mice and A. russatus.
To gain functional insights into immune cell function in aging, we tested the ability of splenocytes to respond to mitogens

To further investigate the underlying molecular landscapes of these age-related pathologies, we performed bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) of young (0.5-year-old) and aged (2.5-year-old) M. musculus and A. russatus.

To do this, we performed single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-seq), an approach that allows examination of adipocytes and the heterogeneity of stromal vascular-immune fraction, in the VAT of M. musculus and A. russatus.

To test this hypothesis, we conducted in vivo experiments using aged (18-month-old) male C57BL/6 mice, which were randomized to receive either vehicle (VEH) or recombinant mouse clusterin (CLU) intraperitoneally for 2 weeks daily
Given these results from in vivo experiments, we further examined whether the anti-inflammaging effects of clusterin were cell autonomous in macrophages.
We next asked whether this anti-inflammatory effect of clusterin can also be translated to human cells.

data.detail: A. russatus maintained all parameters across age groups

source.text: In contrast, A. russatus maintained all these parameters at comparable levels across age groups and did not demonstrate age-related decline or alteration (Fig. 1, E and F, and fig. S1, A to M).

data.detail: A. dimidiatus exhibited age-related decline in rearing behaviors, average speed, traveled distance, and number of entries into the center area

source.text: A. dimidiatus exhibited age-related decline in rearing behaviors, average speed, traveled distance, and number of entries into the center area, which are indicators of increased anxiety and reduced locomotor activity

data.detail: Aged A. russatus exhibited significantly increased latency and freezing time in the wire hanging test and reduced arrival time in the beam walking test

source.text: Moreover, aged A. russatus exhibited significantly increased latency and freezing time in the wire hanging test and reduced arrival time in the beam walking test compared to their young counterparts in both sexes, indicating improved motor and muscular functions with age

data.detail: Aged A. dimidiatus had reduced latency in the wire hanging test

source.text: In contrast, aged A. dimidiatus had reduced latency in the wire hanging test, while other parameters remained unchanged during aging

data.detail: A. russatus did not show disrupted activity patterns during aging

source.text: In contrast, these disruptions were not observed in either sex of A. russatus during aging (Fig. 1, I and J, and fig. S2, J to N).

data.detail: Regeneration capacity declined with age in both species

source.text: Five weeks after ear punches, both adult 0.5-year-old A. dimidiatus and A. russatus exhibited almost completely closed earholes, while regeneration capacity declined with age in both species

data.detail: Aged A. russatus showed improved earhole closure compared to age-matched A. dimidiatus

source.text: Moreover, aged A. russatus showed improved earhole closure compared to age-matched A. dimidiatus (Fig. 1M).

data.detail: Significantly elevated p16 expression in VAT of aged A. dimidiatus but not in A. russatus

source.text: we found significantly elevated p16 expression in the visceral adipose tissues (VAT) of aged A. dimidiatus but not in A. russatus (Fig. 1N and fig. S2S)

data.detail: A. russatus maintained youthful thymic architecture till advanced age, lower lipid accumulation and fibrosis compared to M. musculus

source.text: Notably, compared to laboratory mice, lipid accumulation and fibrosis, key features of thymic involution, were substantially lower in the thymi of age-matched 2.5-year-old A. russatus

data.detail: Sudan Black B–positive senescent-like cells were notably increased in spleens of 2.5-year-old M. musculus, but rarely observed in A. russatus at same age

source.text: We found that Sudan Black B–positive senescent-like cells were notably increased in the spleens of 2.5-year-old M. musculus (Fig. 2, C and E). However, in A. russatus, senescent-like cells were rarely observed in the spleens of 2.5-year-old animals

data.detail: Splenocytes from aged A. russatus showed higher proliferation rate than young, and maintained ConA-induced mitogenic signals

source.text: Splenocytes isolated from aged A. russatus showed a higher proliferation rate than those from young individuals, and aged splenocytes maintained ConA-induced mitogenic signals (Fig. 2G)

data.detail: ConA treatment induced greater expression levels of Il2 and Il4 in splenocytes of A. russatus but not in age-matched M. musculus

source.text: ConA treatment induced greater expression levels of Il2 and Il4 in splenocytes of A. russatus but not in age-matched M. musculus (Fig. 2, J and K).

data.detail: Livers of A. russatus did not show age-related increases in hepatic ballooning, inflammation, and fibrosis

source.text: Similar to the secondary lymphoid organs, the livers of A. russatus did not show age-related increases in hepatic ballooning, inflammation, and fibrosis, which are important phenotypes of aging observed in M. musculus

data.detail: Fewer differentially expressed genes during aging in liver of A. russatus compared to M. musculus

source.text: Notably, we found fewer differentially expressed genes (DEGs) during aging in the liver of A. russatus compared to M. musculus (fig. S4, D and E).

data.detail: Expression levels of SASP and NF-κB gene clusters remained unchanged till 2.5 years of age in A. russatus

source.text: The expression levels of SASP and NF-κB gene clusters remained unchanged till 2.5 years of age in A. russatus (Fig. 3D).

data.detail: Aged A. russatus maintained their CMA score, which was significantly suppressed in M. musculus with age

source.text: Aged A. russatus maintained their CMA score (53), which was significantly suppressed in M. musculus with age (Fig. 3I and fig. S4, N and O).

data.detail: Cells in VAT of aged A. russatus maintained comparable SASP or IASP score except modest increase in ASPCs

source.text: cells in the VAT of aged A. russatus maintained a comparable SASP or IASP score except for a modest increase in ASPCs (Fig. 4F).

data.detail: In VAT of aged A. russatus, macrophages highly expressed clusterin (Clu)

source.text: In the VAT of aged A. russatus, the macrophages highly expressed clusterin (Clu) (Fig. 4J).

data.detail: Clusterin gene expression was up-regulated across cell types in aged A. russatus but not in older M. musculus

source.text: Notably, compared to young animals, the gene expression of clusterin was up-regulated across cell types in aged A. russatus but not in older M. musculus (Fig. 4, K and L).

data.detail: Clusterin administration enhanced grip strength in aged mice compared to VEH controls

source.text: Clusterin administration enhanced measures of health span in aged mice, such as grip strength and latency to fall in rotarod tests, compared to VEH controls

data.detail: Elevation of clusterin reduced fibrosis in gastrocnemius muscle, SAT, spleen, and liver

source.text: elevation of clusterin in aged C57BL/6 mice reduced fibrosis in the gastrocnemius muscle, SAT, spleen, and liver (Fig. 5, F to I)

data.detail: Clusterin reduced circulating IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, and MCP-1

source.text: we found that elevation of clusterin in old mice suppressed the soluble MAC concentration, along with the reduction in circulating proinflammatory cytokines IL-1β, IL-6, and tumor necrosis factor–α (TNF-α) that are known to drive inflammaging

data.detail: Clusterin treatment significantly reduced numbers and frequencies of spleen ABCs and VAT AABs

source.text: recombinant clusterin treatment significantly reduced the numbers and frequencies of spleen ABCs and VAT AABs, and frequencies of VAT M1-like macrophages and VAT Treg cells, while increasing the numbers and frequencies of VAT M2-like macrophages

data.detail: Clusterin reversed age-related increase of hepatic p16, p21, and γ-H2AX

source.text: elevation of clusterin in aged mice reversed the age-related increase of hepatic p16, p21, and γ-H2AX, proteins implicated in controlling cellular senescence–driven organismal aging (Fig. 5P and fig. S9I).

data.detail: Clusterin treatment significantly induced expression of Retnla, Il4, and Il10 in both M1- and M2-polarized BMDMs

source.text: clusterin treatment significantly induced the expression levels of anti-inflammatory genes (Retnla, Il4, and Il10) that are implicated in enhanced tissue repair in both M1- and M2-polarized BMDMs (fig. S9K).

data.parameter: IL-1β and IL-18 production in human monocytes
data.detail: Clusterin treatment significantly reduced IL-1β and IL-18 production in human monocytes in time- and dose-dependent manner

source.text: We observed significant and time- and dose-dependent reduction in inflammasome-regulated cytokine IL-1β and IL-18 production by clusterin treatment in human monocytes (Fig. 5Q and fig. S9M).

data.limitations: Maximal life span of A. russatus remains unclear; limited sample size for sex-specific analysis; differences in husbandry and diet between Acomys and M. musculus

source.text: A limitation of the current study is that, although we endeavored to analyze the health span of A. russatus comprehensively and reported an individual that lived in the wild for more than 3 years and in captivity for more than 4 years, the maximal life span of this species remains unclear.

data.novelty: Identification of A. russatus as a model for aging resistance and clusterin as an immunometabolic resistor

source.text: our findings introduce A. russatus as a model organism for the investigation and identification of targets, such as clusterin, which drive resilience to organismal age-related functional decline.

data.futureResearch: Future studies to identify and characterize adaptokines; comparative analysis of microbial species; well-controlled study to explore maximal life span of A. russatus

source.text: Future studies to identify and characterize adaptokines may reveal mechanisms that drive interorgan communications and maintenance of homeostasis across the life span

data.references: Previous studies on Acomys regeneration, aging atlas, clusterin in Alzheimer's disease, etc.

source.text: Previous studies have identified that three species of spiny mice, Acomys kempi, Acomys dimidiatus, and Acomys percivali, are resistant to poisons and can regenerate their skin
